Naïve-Bayes-Classifier.title: Naïve Bayes Classifier
Naïve-Bayes-Classifier.content:
A naïve Bayes classifier is a supervised machine learning algorithm and a commonly-used variant of the more general Bayes classifier which assumes that features x_{\displaystyle j_{\displaystyle i}} in the feature space X are statistically independent, given each class C_{k}.


                  
                  Need more Detail? 
                  
                

This page covers the specific details of a naïve Bayes classifier. See the dedicated page for Bayes classifiers for a more detailed outline of Bayes classifiers in general.


Such an assumption makes the use of such a classifier more computationally efficient but is often violated when features correlate strongly.
Formula (with Gaussian Assumption)


                  
                  A Note on the Assumed Distribution 
                  
                

The probability distribution we assume depends on the task and the data we have - it doesn’t have to be normally distributed!


Assuming that each feature of X is drawn from a normal distribution, and that each feature x_{i} is statistically independent, given each class C_{k}, we can express the formula for the posterior probability vector P(Y=C_{k}|X) as:
P(Y=C_{k}|X)=\frac{P(X|Y=C_{k})P(Y=C_{k})}{P(X)}
This can be simplified by ignoring the denominator P(X), as this simply a normalisation term which is not necessary for a pure classification task (although it would be needed if the value of P(Y=C_{k}|X) needed to be interpreted directly):
P(Y=C_{k}|X)=P(X|Y=C_{k})P(Y=C_{k})

P(Y=C_{k}), the prior probability of each class, is just estimated by using the relative frequency of each class.
We can express P(X|Y=C_{k}) using some assumed probability density function, such as a normal distribution [x_{i}|C_{k}] \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}):

P(X|Y=C_{k})=\prod_{i=i}^{n}P(x_{i}|C_{k})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_{ki}^{2}}}e^{\displaystyle -\frac{(x_{i}-\mu_{ki})^{2}}{2\sigma_{ki}^{2}}}

Sample

r_{xy}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}-\bar{x})(y_{i}-\bar{y})}{\displaystyle \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}-n\bar{x}^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}^{2}-n\bar{y}^{2}}}

Perplexity.title: Perplexity
Perplexity.content:
In information theory, the perplexity of a discrete probability distribution is the number of equally likely outcomes in a uniform distribution whose entropy equals the entropy of the given distribution.
Perplexity is closely related to Shannon entropy - that is, it is the exponential of the Shannon entropy.
Formula
The perplexity of a discrete probability distribution of a random variable X is given by:
\text{PP}(X)=e^{H(X)}
Where H(X) is the Shannon entropy of X, measured in nats.
Applications
Natural Language Processing
In natural language processing, the perplexity of a sequence of words is given by the inverse probability of that sequence, normalised by the number of words n:
\text{PP}(W)=P(w_{1},\dots,w_{n})^{\displaystyle-1/n}=e^{\displaystyle-1/n\times\log(P(w_{1},\dots,w_{n}))}
This gives us a means of assessing the performance of a language model. For example, we can compare N-gram models by measuring their perplexity on a test text corpus and seeing which model has the lowest perplexity (i.e. the best at returning the highest probability next word).

Pointwise-Mutual-Information.title: Pointwise Mutual Information

In natural language processing, we can find the PMI of seeing a word and some feature occurring together in a text.
Formula
For some feature f and some word w, their PMI is found by taking the number of times the feature and the word occur together in a text, multiplying this by the total number of word-feature occurrences for all word-feature pairs and then dividing this by the product of the number of occurrences of the word and the number of occurrences of the feature:
I(f,w)=\log\frac{P(f|w)}{P(f)}=\log\frac{P(f \cap w)}{P(f)\times P(w)}=\log\frac{\text{freq}(f,w)\times\text{freq}_{\text{tot}}}{\text{freq}_{\text{word}}\times\text{freq}_{\text{feature}}}
Positive PMI
If frequencies are 0, we would have an undefined value. Thus, we can instead return 0 in the case when I(f,w) <= 0:
\text{PPMI}(f,w)=\begin{cases} I(f,w) & I(f,w) > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

ROC-Curve.title: ROC Curve
ROC-Curve.content:
The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve is a plot used to compare the true positive rate (TPR) to the false positive rate (FPR) across a range of decision thresholds for a binary classification machine learning algorithm.
Interpretation
Plotting the TPR and FPR produces an ROC curve. Below is an example

We can interpret this plot in a couple of ways to learn about our model:

The area under the ROC curve (AUC) tells us, given a pair of positive and negative labelled data points, the probability that the model will assign a higher probability of belonging to the positive class to the actual positive data point rather than to the negative data point.

For example:

If the AUC is 0.5 then the model essentially flips a coin to decide which data point (the actual positive or actual negative) to assign a higher probability of being positive to.
An AUC of 1 would always correctly assign a higher probability of being positive to the actual positive data point.




The points on the curve which is closest to the co-ordinate (0,1) are the range of optimal thresholds to choose for the classification model.

If we want to avoid false positives, we can choose a point on the curve which has the lowest FPR. Likewise, if we want to avoid false negatives, we could choose the point with the highest TPR.

Softmax-Function.title: Softmax Function
Softmax-Function.content:
The softmax function is a generalisation of the logistic function to multidimensional cases.
Softmax is used in multinomial logistic regression and as an activation function in neural networks, particularly for the output layer.
Formula
\sigma(z_{i})=\frac{e^{z_{i}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}e^{z_{j}}}\quad \text{where }k>1

Spearman's-Rank-Correlation-Coefficient.title: Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient
Spearman's-Rank-Correlation-Coefficient.content:
Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, also known as Spearman’s \rho, is a particular rank correlation measure used to measure the linear relationship between two ordinal variables.
Formula
Given some sample of n pairs of data \{(x_{1}, y_{1}), \dots, (x_{n}, y_{n})\} drawn from two random variables X and Y, we can convert each value to be a rank relative to its respective variable (R[X_{i}], R[Y_{i}]).

For example, if we had a sample \{0.4, 0.9, 0.1, 0.7, 0.2\}, we could convert each value to be its rank within this sample: \{3, 5, 1, 4, 2\}.

Thus, the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient r_{s} is found in an analogous manner to the population Pearson correlation coefficient, except using ranked variables, by dividing the covariance of the ranked variables by the product of their standard deviations:
r_{s}=\frac{\text{cov}[R[X],R[Y]]}{\sigma_{R[X]}\sigma_{R[Y]}}
If the n pairs of ranks all contain distinct integers, then we can find r_{s} using the following expression:
r_{s}=1-\frac{\displaystyle6\sum_{i}(R[X_{i}]-R[Y_{i}])^{2}}{n(n^{2}-1)}

Square-Matrix.title: Square Matrix
Square-Matrix.content:
A square matrix is a matrix where the number of rows m is equal to the number of columns n.
Types
Triangular Matrix
A triangular matrix is a square matrix where all the elements either above or below the main diagonal are equal to 0.

Standard-Normal-Distribution.title: Standard Normal Distribution
Standard-Normal-Distribution.content:
The standard normal distribution is a normal distribution with mean \mu=0 and variance \sigma^{2}=1
This standard normal distribution is incredibly useful, allowing us to standardise any normal distribution by converting its values to z-scores, allowing us to find the probabilities associated with certain ranges of values in our distribution.
Without this standard normal distribution, such probabilities would need to be uniquely found for each unique normal distribution - of which there are infinitely many.
Notation
The standard normal distribution is denoted by:
\mathcal{N}(0,1)

Standardised-Moments.title: Standardised Moments
Standardised-Moments.content:
Standardised moments of the probability distribution of a random variable are the central moments of that distribution, standardised by some integer power of the standard deviation of that distribution.
The 1^{st} and 2^{nd} standardised moments are equal to 0 and 1, respectively.
The 3^{rd} and 4^{th} standardised moments are equivalent to the skewness and kurtosis, respectively.
Formula
The k^{th} standardised moment \bar{\mu}_{k} of the probability distribution of a random variable is given by:
\bar{\mu}_{k} = \frac{E[(X-\mu)^{k}]}{E[(X-\mu)^{2}]^{k/2}}
Where E[(X-\mu)^{2}]^{k/2} is the k^{th} power of the standard deviation of that distribution \sigma^{k}.

Stationary-Distribution.title: Stationary Distribution
Stationary-Distribution.content:
A stationary distribution of a Markov chain is a probability distribution of states in the chain which remains unchanged as the time step k increases.
Notation
Some probability mass function \pi is a stationary distribution if, when multiplied with a transition matrix P:
\pi P=\pi
We can also express the stationary distribution as:
\pi(X_{k})=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\pi(X_{j})p_{jk}~~~~~\forall j,k \in \mathcal{S}

Statistical-Error.title: Statistical Error
Statistical-Error.content:
A statistical error is defined as the difference between an observed value and the true population value.

Stochastic-Gradient-Descent.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent
Stochastic-Gradient-Descent.content:
Stochastic gradient descent is a variation of the gradient descent algorithm where the gradient is calculated at each time step on a random subset of the data, rather than the entire data set.
Such a method requires less computation at each iteration, but can increase the number of iterations needed to converge on optimal weights.
Formula
The weights at time t+1 is given by subtracting the sum of the gradient at each i^{\text{th}} data point in the subset B from the weights at time t:
w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}-\eta \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\frac{\partial \ell(f(x_{i}),y_{i})}{\partial w}

Strength-(Graphs).title: Strength (Graphs)
Strength-(Graphs).content:
In the context of graphs, if the graph is weighted then we can, for a given vertex, find the strength of that vertex.
Formula
For an undirected weighted graph, the strength s_{i} of a vertex is given by:
s_{i}=\sum_{i}w_{ij}

Stride.title: Stride
Stride.content:
Stride, in the context of convolutional neural networks, refers to how many elements a kernel moves by in each iteration of a scan across some input matrix.
Increasing stride length results in fewer computations and is thus more efficient, but loses information as not all subsets of the elements in the input matrix. Nonetheless, we might want a larger stride length if we want to capture more global patterns in our input matrix, or a shorter stride length if we want more granular detail.

References

Strong-Communities-(Graphs).title: Strong Communities (Graphs)
Strong-Communities-(Graphs).content:
A strong community is a subgraph of a graph where the in-degree of each vertex in the subgraph is greater than its out-degree.
We can also define a strong community in probabilistic terms:

A strong community is a subgraph where each vertex has a higher probability of being connected to each of the other vertices in the subgraph compared to any other vertex in the graph.

Notation
Given a subgraph G_{r}, the subgraph is a strong community if:
k_{i}^{\text{in}}(G_{r}) > k_{i}^{\text{out}}(G_{r})\quad\forall i\in G_{r}

References

Stupid-Backoff.title: Stupid Backoff
Stupid-Backoff.content:
In natural language processing, the stupid backoff algorithm is a technique to find the relative frequencies of n-grams in a corpus.
This method ignores the requirement to normalise frequencies such that they form a valid probability distribution (hence the adjective “stupid”).
Formula
If the n-gram has a probability >0, use its relative frequency, otherwise “backoff” to the n-1-gram, multiply by a fixed weight \lambda (usually \lambda=0.4, see Brants et al. (2007)) and check again.
S\left(w_{\displaystyle i}|w_{\displaystyle i-k+1}^{\displaystyle i-1}\right)=\begin{cases}\frac{\displaystyle\text{count}\left(w_{\displaystyle i-k+1}^{\displaystyle i}\right)}{\displaystyle\text{count}\left(w_{\displaystyle i-k+1}^{\displaystyle i-1}\right)} &\text{if count}\left(w_{\displaystyle i-k+1}^{\displaystyle i}\right)>0\\ \\ \lambda S\left(w_{\displaystyle i}|w_{\displaystyle i-k+2}^{\displaystyle i-1}\right) &\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

Sum-of-Squared-Differences.title: Sum of Squared Differences
Sum-of-Squared-Differences.content:
The sum of squared differences is a measure of the discrepancy between two sets of values, elements by element.
If the squared differences being compared are predicted values to true values (i.e. residuals) in a machine learning model (e.g. linear regression), we refers to a particular instance of the sum of squared differences, namely the sum of squared residuals.

References

Sum-of-Squared-Residuals.title: Sum of Squared Residuals
Sum-of-Squared-Residuals.content:
The sum of squared residuals is a measure of the overall amount of deviation between the observed values in a dataset and the estimated values made by a model, which is simply the sum of each squared observed-estimated value.
Squaring these residuals ensures that positive and negative signs do not cancel out. Since we only care about the magnitude of the deviation, not the direction per-se, we square each residual to ensure it is a positive value.

Supervised-Learning.title: Supervised Learning
Supervised-Learning.content:
Supervised learning refers to a type of machine learning algorithm where a model is trained on a dataset with some pre-existing labels which can be used to inform the model (via a loss function) of how to most optimally map input data to correct output values.
The general task, therefore, for supervised learning algorithms is to find optimal model parameters which minimise some loss function by using examples of correct pairs of input and output data.

Support-Vector-Machine-(SVM).title: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
Support-Vector-Machine-(SVM).content:
uA support vector machine (SVM) is a supervised machine learning model used for classification  and continuous-output prediction tasks.
SVMs aim to find a hyperplane which maximises the margin between two classes whilst still correctly classifying each data point into its appropriate class in the feature space. This hyperplane is therefore at the midpoint between the two classes.
Hyperplanes and Marginal Distance
We can express an equation for the marginal hyperplane as follows:
w^{\top}x+b=0
This marginal hyperplane is just the midpoint between the two classes in the feature space.
The marginal hyperplane’s corresponding positive and negative hyperplanes are:
\begin{align}
\text{Positive:}~~~~~w^{\top}x+b&=1 \\
\text{Negative:}~~~~~w^{\top}x+b&=-1
\end{align}
With SVMs, we want to maximise the marginal distance - that is, the distance between the positive and negative hyperplanes. This distance is found by subtracting the negative hyperplane from the positive hyperplane:
w^{\top}x_{\text{positive}}+b - w^{\top}x_{\text{negative}}+b = 1 - (-1)
Simplifying:
w^{\top}(x_{\text{positive}} - x_{\text{negative}}) = 2
We can divide by the norm of w to cancel out w^{\top}:
\frac{w^{\top}}{||w||}(x_{\text{positive}}-x_{\text{negative}})=x_{\text{positive}}-x_{\text{negative}}=\frac{2}{||w||}
Thus, maximising \displaystyle\frac{2}{||w||} will find the optimal hyperplane.

Similarly, minimising \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}||w^{2}|| will find the optimal hyperplane.

Loss Function
Primal Formulation
L_{\text{SVM}}(W)=-\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_{n}(y_{n}(\mathbf{x}_{n}\mathbf{w})-1)+\frac{1}{2}||\mathbf{w}||^{2}
Where:

\beta_{n} are Lagrange multipliers
y_{n} is

Dual Formulation
g(\beta)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_{n}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n,m=1}^{N}\beta_{n}\beta_{m}y_{n}y_{m}\mathbf{x}_{n}\mathbf{x}_{m}~,~~~~~\beta_{n}\ge0

Surjection.title: Surjective
Surjection.content:
Surjection is a function which maps elements from set A to set B such that every element in B is paired with at least 1 element in A. Thus, with surjection, elements in B can be paired with more than one element in A, but not vice-versa.
Notation
To define surjection, we can say that for every element in B, there exists an element in A such that there is function which maps at least one element in A to that element in B and only that element in B:
\forall b \in B, \exists a \in A ~|~ f(a)=b

Synonymy.title: Synonymy
Synonymy.content:
Synonymy describes a relationship between words where each word means the same thing as every other word.
Words are synonymous if they can be substituted in all possible context without changing the meaning of the sentence.
True synonyms are very rare. Instead, we colloquially refer to words as synonyms if they have one or more shared word senses.

References

The-Distributional-Hypothesis.title: The Distributional Hypothesis
The-Distributional-Hypothesis.content:
The distributional hypothesis, as formulated by Harris (1954) stipulates that:

“Words that occur in the same contexts tend to have similar meanings.” - Harris (1954)

This hypothesis forms a key assumption underlying distributional semantics.

References

www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/00437956.1954.11659520

Transition-Matrix.title: Transition Matrix
Transition-Matrix.content:
A transition matrix is a square matrix used to describe the transition probabilities of a Markov chain.
Notation
Let P be a transition matrix and let our Markov chain have i\in\{1,\dots,n\} states. We can express the probabilities of moving from state i to any state j using a transition matrix:
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
P_{1,1} & P_{1,2} & \dots & P_{1,j} & \dots & P_{1,n} \\ 
P_{2,1} & P_{1,2} & \dots & P_{2,j} & \dots & P_{2,n} \\ 
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 
P_{i,1} & P_{i,2} & \dots & P_{i,j} & \dots & P_{i,n} \\ 
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 
P_{n,1} & P_{n,2} & \dots & P_{n,j} & \dots & P_{i,n} \\
\end{pmatrix}
~~~~~~~~~~\text{where }\sum_{j=1}^{n}P_{i,j}=1
The k-step probability of moving from i to j is simply found by finding P^{k} and looking up the (i,j)^{\text{th}} element.

For example, if we wanted to know the probability of moving from state 3 to state 7 in 5 time steps, we would find P^{5} and look up probability value at the element (3,5).

Transitivity.title: Transitivity
Transitivity.content:
Transitivity is the probability that two vertices, which are adjacent to some reference vertex, in a graph share an edge between them.
Formula
The transitivity T can be found by dividing the number of closed triplets by the total number of triplets:
T=\frac{N_{\text{closed triplets}}}{N_{\text{all triplets}}}

Triplet-(Graphs).title: Triplet (Graphs)
Triplet-(Graphs).content:
A triplet is structure in a graph, where three vertices are connected by edges.
Types
Open Triplet
An open triplet consists of three vertices which are connected by at least two edges.
Closed Triplet
A closed triplet is where all three vertices respectively share an edge.

1 closed triplet is equivalent to 3 triangles. For any set of 3 vertices \{A,B,C\}, we can express three versions of the same triangle, each cantered at a vertex in the set: (ABC, BCA, CBA).

True-Negatives.title: True Negatives
True-Negatives.content:
A true negative refers to a prediction made by a classification machine learning algorithm where the model correctly identifies that the data does not belong to a particular class.

True-Positives.title: True Positives
True-Positives.content:
A true positive refers to a prediction made by a classification machine learning algorithm where the predicted class of some data matches the true class.

Uncountable-Set.title: Uncountable Set
Uncountable-Set.content:
An uncountable set is a set with a cardinality greater than that of the natural numbers.

Undersampling.title: Undersampling
Undersampling.content:
Undersampling is a technique used to address class imbalance in the dataset used to train a classification machine learning algorithm by reducing the number of samples in the majority classes.
Undersampling can be achieved by removing random samples from the majority classes such that the number of samples equals that of the minority class.

Union.title: Union
Union.content:
The union of two sets A and B is the set of all the elements in A and all the elements in B.
If there are duplicated elements between A and B, only one instance of these duplicated elements is added to the union.
Notation
For two sets, we can define their union as all the set of all elements that are either in A or in B. This is denoted as follows:
A \cup B=\{x:x\in A \lor x \in B\}
For n sets A_{1},\dots,A_{n}, their union is denoted as:
\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}=A_{1}\cup A_{2} \cup \dots \cup A_{n-1} \cup A_{n}=\{x ~|~ \exists i \in \{1,\dots,n\} ~|~ x \in A_{i}\}

Unit-Imputation.title: Unit Imputation
Unit-Imputation.content:
Unit imputation is a method for handling missing data in a dataset.
Types

Upper-Incomplete-Gamma-Function.title: Upper Incomplete Gamma Function
Upper-Incomplete-Gamma-Function.content:
The upper incomplete gamma function is a type of gamma function with a lower integral limit of x, rather than 0.
Formula
\Gamma(s,x)=\int_{x}^{\infty}t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt

References

Variance.title: Variance
Variance.content:
Variance is a measure of dispersion, defined as the expected value of the squared deviation from the mean of a random variable, which indicates how close data points are to their average value.
As the units of the variances are always the squared units of the data it is calculated on (e.g. data in meters \therefore variance in meters-squared), we can instead make use of the square root of the variance, known as the standard deviation, which is often more intuitive.
Formulae
The variance of a random variable X is given by the expectation of the squared difference between X and the mean \mu:
\text{Var}(X)=E\left[(X-\mu)^{2}\right]
For a discrete random variable, we can find the variance by weighting the squared difference between the value of x and the mean \mu by the probability of x_{i} (denoted p_{i}):
\text{Var}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}(x_{i}-\mu)^{2}
For a continuous random variable, for some probability density function f(x), we can evaluate the following integral:
\text{Var}(X)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^{2}f(x)\,dx-\mu^{2}
We can also define the variance as the covariance of X with itself:
\text{Var}(X)=\text{Cov}(X,X)

References

Vector-Space.title: Vector Space
Vector-Space.content:
A vector space refers to a set of vectors which can be scaled by scalars.

References

Vector.title: Vector
Vector.content:
A vector is a mathematical object, represented by an array of ordered values, which has some magnitude and direction in a co-ordinate space.
Notation
In data science, vectors are typically denoted using bold letters like \mathbf{x}. A vector is an array of ordered values, like such:
\mathbf{x}=\left[1,0.5,\sqrt{43},\pi,\dots\right]
If the vector represents a sample in a dataset, then each element corresponds to a value that vector has for a particular feature.
Column and Row Vectors
We can express vectors as columns or rows, which alters how the vector interacts with other objects in mathematical operations. For example, in matrix-vector multiplication, a row vector multiplied with a matrix yields a 1\times m row vector:
\begin{bmatrix}a&b&c\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\alpha & \beta \\ \gamma & \delta \\ \epsilon & \zeta\end{bmatrix}=[a\alpha+b\beta+c\gamma,\,a\delta+b\epsilon+c\zeta]
Whereas a column vector multiplied with a matrix yields an m\times 1 column vector:
\begin{bmatrix}\alpha & \beta & \gamma \\ \delta & \epsilon & \zeta\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\\c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a\alpha+b\beta+c\gamma \\ \,a\delta+b\epsilon+c\zeta\end{bmatrix}

References

Vertex.title: Vertex
Vertex.content:
In the context of graphs, a vertex represents an object within a given graph.
The collection of all vertices in a graph G is given by |V|
Degree
The number of edges connected to a vertex is called the vertex’s degree
Strength
For an undirected weighted graph, we can find the strength of a vertex s_{i} by summing all the weights of the edges connected to it:
s_{i}=\sum_{i}w_{ij}

References

Watts-Strogatz-Model.title: Watts-Strogatz Model
Watts-Strogatz-Model.content:
The Watts-Strogatz model is a type of random graph which can be used to produce small-world networks.
Algorithm
Given some number of vertices N, a mean degree k, and some probability of rewiring each edge p:

Create a regular ring lattice out the the N vertices.

This means the vertices are arranged into a circle and each vertex is wired to k neighbours, with an even number (or close to even if k is odd) of neighbours to the left and right of that vertex.


For each vertex i:

For each of its k/2 rightmost neighbours j:

Rewire the edge between i and j to some other vertex k \neq i in the network with probability p





Properties
Expected Number of Rewired Edges
The expected number of rewired edges is just half of the product of the number of vertices N, the mean degree k and the probability of rewiring p:
pL=\frac{pNk}{2}
Small-Worldedness
With Watts-Strogatz graphs, we can find a probability of rewiring p such that the average path length is low and the clustering coefficient is high.
These are the properties of small-world networks, and so the Watts-Strogatz model can be used to randomly generate such graphs.
We can consider a small-world index to measure the extent to which a randomly generated Watts-Strogatz graph conforms to the properties of a small-world network.

References

Weak-Communities-(Graphs).title: Weak Communities (Graphs)
Weak-Communities-(Graphs).content:
A weak community is a subgraph of a graph where sum of the in-degrees of each vertex in the subgraph is greater than the sum of the out-degrees
We can also define a weak community in probabilistic terms:

A weak community is a subgraph where each vertex has a higher average probability of being connected to each of the other vertices in the subgraph compared to the average probability of being connected to any other vertex in the graph.

Notation
Given a subgraph G_{r}, the subgraph is a weak community if:
\sum_{i\in G_{r}}k_{i}^{\text{in}}(G_{r}) > \sum_{i\in G_{r}}k_{i}^{\text{out}}(G_{r})\quad\forall i\in G_{r}

References

Word-Embeddings.title: Word Embeddings
Word-Embeddings.content:
A word embedding is a fixed-dimensional vector representation of a word used in neural networks.
For some set of words in a corpus, we can consider each of their word embedding vectors as a row in an embedding matrix. The values of this embedding matrix are therefore a set of parameters learned by the neural network during training.

References

Word-Sense.title: Word Sense
Word-Sense.content:
A word sense is one of the meanings of a word.

References

Word2Vec.title: Word2Vec
Word2Vec.content:
Word2Vec is a method in Natural Language Processing which uses neural networks to learn word embeddings from a large corpus of text.
Given some current word (called the target word), we can consider a context window around that word (e.g. the 2 words before and the 2 words after the target word).
Each word is then given two embeddings:

Target embedding: an embedding for when the word is the target word,
Context embedding: an embedding for when the word is a context word.

Architectures
Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)
The continuous bag of words (CBOW) architecture aims to predict a word given its surrounding context.
To predict a word, CBOW uses the sum (or average) of the context embeddings for the surrounding words to predict target embedding of the target word.

Training
We can then assess how close our predicted target embedding was to the true embedding from a corpus and backpropagate the error to update the values of the elements in context embeddings.
Skip-Gram
The skip-gram architecture aims to predict the surrounding context given some word.
CBOW uses a target embedding to predict the context embeddings.

Training
Skip-gram takes a target word and aims to predict the context words surrounding it within some context window.
The loss function used for skip-gram maximises the probability of true pairs of words and maximises the probability that false pairs are labelled negative.
This is achieved by finding the dot product of the target word t and one of its context words c and passing it to a sigmoid activation function. The result is therefore the probability that c is a true context word of t.
We therefore want our skip-gram model to output large probabilities for true (t,c) pairs and small probabilities for false (t,c) pairs. The embeddings for t and c are therefore still learned via gradient descent.
J=\sum_{(t,c)\in +} \sigma(c \cdot t) + \sum_{(t,c)\in -} \sigma(-c \cdot t)

References

arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781

WordNet.title: WordNet
WordNet.content:
WordNet is a large lexical database in which words are grouped into sets called synsets.
Synsets
Synsets are a collection of words which share a common word sense.
Words can be in more than one synset (called polysemous words).
Synsets can be placed into a hierarchy
Concept Similarity Using Synsets
Path Length
Finding the path length between two concepts in a hyponym hierarchy is a matter of counting the number of edges traversed along the shortest path between two concepts.
We can then use this pathlength to find an expression for the similarity of the two concepts:
\text{sim}_{\text{path}}(c_{1}, c_{2}) = \frac{1}{1+\text{pathlen}(c_{1}, c_{2})}
Disadvantages

Path length doesn’t differentiate between different types of paths in the hierarchy
Concepts separated by the same path length may be more dissimilar at higher levels of the hierarchy than those lower down.

Lowest Common Subsumer
The lowest common subsumer (LCS) is the lowest-level hypernym two concepts share in a hyponym hierarchy.
Concepts in the hierarchy which share an LCS which is higher up the hierarchy are less similar than concept which share an LCS lower down the hierarchy.
Information Content
We can also get a sense of how informative a concept is.
If we find two concepts share a LCS which is lower down the hierarchy, we get more information about how alike the two concepts are than if their LCS is higher up the hierarchy.
By finding the total number of occurrences of a concept and all its hyponyms and dividing this by the total number of occurrences of all concepts in the hierarchy, we can estimate the probability of that concept occurring.
The negative log of this probability gives us the information content of that concept.
From this notion of information content, we have the following measures of concept similarity in WordNet:

Resnik Similarity
Lin Similarity
Jiang-Conrath Similarity


References

Z-scores.title: Z-scores
Z-scores.content:
A z-score is a normalised value used to indicate the number of standard deviations away from the mean a given raw value is.
Formula
For some mean \mu and some standard deviation \sigma, the z-score of some data point x is given by:
z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}

Zipf's-Law.title: Zipf's Law
Zipf's-Law.content:
Ziph’s law refers to an empirical phenomenon which occurs in a wide range of contexts where, by sorting a set of measurements in descending order, we find that the value of the n-th measurement is proportional to 1/n.
Examples
Word Frequency in a Text
If we count the number of times each word appears in a text and sort them in descending order by word count, we find that the word count of the 2^{nd} most common word is about 1/2 the value of the most common word.
The 3^{rd} most common word therefore occurs 1/3 as often as the most common word; the 4^{th} most common word occurs 1/4 as often as the most common word, and so on…
This phenomenon occurs for any body of text which represent natural language.
